card_title: Physics-informed neural networks for ODE-based dynamic optimisation in chemical processes
full_title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for ODE-based Dynamic Optimization in Chemical Processes
card_text: Uses physics-informed neural networks to optimise four chemical processes described by ODEs, learning control and state profiles together; it set new best values on two of the four.
details_md:
## Abstract

**Purpose.** Industry-grade biochemical reactors require dynamic optimization to maximize yield, minimize costs etc. Complex relationships between interrelated variables, expressed as ODE systems, are optimized for a given objective function – traditionally using discrete and intelligent optimization methods. Building on our previous work in DNN-based optimization, this paper explores the use of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for dynamic chemical optimization.

**Methods.** PINNs are deep neural networks trained to model physical systems (here, ODE systems representing chemical processes) by approximating the mathematical relationships between the different variables. For a network that predicts control and state variable profiles, the objective loss (optimizes the objective function) and the physics loss (ensures the mathematical system is obeyed) are simultaneously minimized. Our network thus learns the optimal objective function value while still obeying the underlying mathematical system.

**Results.** We evaluate our PINNs methodology with four real world dynamic chemical optimization problems, and compare our results with our previous work in DNNs, as well as with other literature. Our physics losses are marginal (< 0.1 for three of the four case studies). Furthermore, our PINNs are able to achieve high resultant objective function values, and outperform existing literature for two of the four case studies (setting new best values).

**Conclusion.** For at least three of the four case studies evaluated, we conclude that PINNs are capable of not just modelling the underlying mathematical systems, but also optimizing the objective functions as well as (if not better than) existing optimization methods. Although limitations in capturing erratic function profiles and minimizing tiny consistent error terms remain, PINNs improve upon our DNNs in two ways: modelling state variables (not just control variables), and achieving better objective function values. We propose evaluating more advanced architectures and a wider range of chemical problems for our future work.
keywords: Physics-Informed ML;Optimisation & Control;ML for Physical Systems

card_title: Deep neural networks for ODE-based dynamic optimisation in chemical processes
full_title: Deep Neural Networks for ODE-Based Dynamic Optimization in Chemical Processes
venue: International Conference on Data Management, Analytics and Innovation (ICDMAI), Springer
card_text: Trains deep neural networks with a Runge-Kutta solver to learn smooth control profiles for four chemical-process problems, with results comparable to state-of-the-art discrete methods.
details_md:
## Abstract

Dynamic Optimization is an important topic in chemically and biochemically reacting systems, notably prevalent in optimizing chemical/biochemical reactors for maximizing yield, minimizing cost etc. The high-dimensional and complex nature of chemical processes makes it extremely difficult to ascertain analytically optimal solutions for such a wide range of problems. As such, machine learning-based approaches are employed to solve and obtain the optimal trajectory of control variables in the chemical process. Traditionally, discrete optimization techniques are employed for the task of solving ODE-based Dynamic Optimization problems, which work by converting a continuous range of values into a discrete set of points, through which a trajectory must be optimized. In this paper, we explore and evaluate the application of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in solving such chemical/biochemical problems. Combined with the Runge-Kutta 4th order method of ODE approximation, DNNs are trained to learn a smooth and continuous function representation of the control variable over time, which, for a given system of ODE constraints, optimizes the specified objective. We test our proposed methodology on four real world-based case studies and compare our results with other literature employing traditional discrete optimization methods. A comparison of the results obtained reveals that the proposed DNN-based methodology yields results comparable to those obtained from state-of-the-art discrete methods. We further discuss some challenges and limitations faced in our methodology and potential ways to mitigate them, including the difficulty of DNNs in capturing non-smooth function profiles, and the handling of boundary constraints on variables in the chemical process. Finally, we raise a call for research into further evaluations and applications of neural networks in solving dynamic optimization problems, including the employment of hybrid models and advanced neural network architectures.
keywords: Optimisation & Control;Deep Learning;ML for Physical Systems

card_title: Minority class oversampling using random forest proximity matrix and genetic algorithms
full_title: Minority Class Oversampling using Random Forest Proximity Matrix and Genetic Algorithms
venue: International Conference on Data Management, Analytics and Innovation (ICDMAI), Springer
card_text: A new oversampling method for imbalanced data, built on random forest proximities, with genetic algorithms to pick synthetic examples; it consistently beat SMOTE baselines across 18 benchmark datasets.
details_md:
## Abstract

Supervised Machine Learning algorithms perform best by employing balanced datasets, i.e. datasets where each class has an equal (or comparable) number of examples to learn from. In contrast, real life tasks such as anomaly or rare-event detection rarely have balanced datasets available. Imbalanced data can cause biases towards the majority class, leading to poorer classification performances. As such, class balancing is an important task in data pre-processing. Oversampling techniques such as SMOTE work by interpolating and synthesizing artificial minority-class examples. In this paper, we employ Random Forests and their associated Proximity Matrices to propose a novel oversampling technique: Random Forest Proximity-based Oversampling (RF-POS). We elaborate our methodology and compare its effectiveness in classification tasks with traditional SMOTE for 18 benchmark datasets. We further propose Genetic Algorithms (GA) for learning synthetic example selection strategies, and evaluate the effectiveness of its addition to different oversampling techniques. We also compare GA with a simple class probability-based example selection method. Our results demonstrate that RF-POS handles complex and highly imbalanced datasets better than SMOTE. Moreover, RF-POS with GA-based example selection consistently outperforms the SMOTE baselines (both with/without synthetic example selection), and obtains the best classification performances.

card_title: Detecting depression: employing word-embeddings and sentence transformers
full_title: Detecting depression: employing word-embeddings and sentence transformers
venue: Journal of Computational Social Science, Springer Nature
card_text: Detects depression in Reddit posts using word embeddings and sentence transformers; the best model reaches an F1 score of 98.04%, up from a 93.24% TF-IDF baseline.
details_md:
## Abstract

Detecting Depression in individuals can prevent significant amounts of mental anguish. This study expands on our previous work, “Detecting Depression: Employing Natural Language Processing and Random Forests”, and further explores the potential of machine learning in detecting Depression from text. Previously, we curated a dataset of 291 Depression and 698 Control text posts obtained from Reddit. Using TF-IDF features, we trained Random Forest classifiers and achieved an F1 score of 93.24% and an accuracy of 93.21%. Treating this as our baseline, we now evaluate GLoVe word embeddings and Sentence Transformer models for feature extraction. We employ Random Forest, Logistic Regression and Multi-Layer Perceptron classifiers for supervised classification. Our results show that GLoVe embeddings outperform the baseline (F1 score: 94.91%, accuracy: 94.79%). Additionally, our four Sentence Transformers (All MiniLM L6 v2, All MPNet base v2, GTR T5 base and Sentence T5 base) achieve substantially higher results. Our best-performing model uses All MPNet base v2 base transformer embeddings, SMOTE class balancing and a tuned Random Forest classifier to achieve an F1 score of 98.04% and a classification accuracy of 98.07%, outperforming state-of-the-art transformers such as DepRoBERTa. Finally, we discuss the possibility of real-world and clinical applications, along with the various associated ethical considerations and caveats.

card_title: Global music recommendation using deep contrastive learning and hybridised filtering
full_title: Global Music Recommendation using Deep Contrastive Learning and Hybridized Filtering
venue: International Conference on Innovation in Computing and Engineering (ICE), IEEE, Delhi
card_text: A music recommender that combines content-based and collaborative filtering through deep contrastive learning; it outperformed both baselines and can recommend Hindi songs to English-speaking listeners.
details_md:
## Abstract

Music is a significant part of any culture’s identity, and has the power to connect people with cultures across the globe. In this paper, we introduce and evaluate a novel Hybridized Filtering approach for Music Recommendation, implemented by employing a Deep Contrastive Learning methodology. We evaluate and compare our proposed methodology to existing and popular recommendation approaches: namely Content-based and Collaborative Filtering. By evaluating the performance metric AURC: Area Under the Recall@K vs K Curve, we conclude that our new approach has a better recommendation performance than the alternatives. We explain how this approach handles and mitigates numerous limitations associated with the others. Furthermore, we demonstrate our model’s ability to provide Global recommendations by recommending songs in a new language (Hindi) for an English user.

card_title: Detecting depression: employing natural language processing and random forests
full_title: Detecting Depression: Employing Natural Language Processing and Random Forests
venue: Congress on Smart Computing Technologies (CSCT 2023), Springer
card_text: Detects depression in Reddit posts with TF-IDF features and random forests; on a curated set of 989 posts, the best model reaches an F1 score of 93.24%.
details_md:
## Abstract

Depression is not just a sad feeling, but a serious mental illness. This paper seeks to use Machine Learning to predict Depression in a given text. Based on the idea that text written by sufferers of Depression differs from text written by persons without depression, we seek to extract Natural Language Processing features (namely Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency or TF-IDF features) from a dataset of texts written by Depressed and non-Depressed people. We employ these features, and train supervised learning (Random Forest) classification models to classify the text into one of two different classes: Depressed and non-Depressed. We also perform varying levels of Mutual Information-based Feature Selection of the TF-IDF features to compare and analyse the effects of feature selection on the performance of our models. By using our curated dataset of anonymized text posts from Reddit (291 Depression and 698 Control posts), our best model achieves a classification F1-Score of 93.24% and a classification accuracy of 93.21% on a test dataset, serving as a testament to the various possibilities of using Machine Learning in the field of detecting mental illnesses and disorders (Depression and similar disorders) at a larger scale.

card_title: A novel technique for rain/no-rain classification using outgoing longwave radiation data from INSAT-3D
full_title: A Novel Technique for Rain/No-Rain Classification Using Outgoing Longwave Radiation Data from INSAT-3D
venue: IEEE India Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (InGARSS), IEEE
card_text: Detects rainfall over the Indian subcontinent from INSAT-3D satellite radiation data with random forests, beating two operational methods: a Critical Success Index of 0.41, against 0.25 and 0.31.
details_md:
## Abstract

This study presents a novel approach for rainfall detection over the Indian subcontinent using INSAT-3D Outgoing Longwave Radiation (OLR) data and Random Forest classification. We employed the Random Forest classifier, experimenting with various hyperparameters to optimize performance. We utilized data from June 2021, covering the region 0N-40N and 60E-100E, with Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP) as reference. Our model, trained on 80% of the data and validated through five-fold cross-validation, outperforms operational methods in Critical Success Index and Equitable Threat Score. Notably, our approach demonstrated superior performance compared to two existing models, the Hydro-Estimator method (HE) and the INSAT Multispectral Rainfall Algorithm (IMSRA). Our proposed method achieved a Critical Success Index(CSI) value of 0.41 and Equitable Threat Score(ETS) value of 0.39 which represent an improvement over the corresponding values for HE(0.25 and 0.23) and IMSRA (0.31 and 0.30).

card_title: PID control for feature selection in biomedical datasets
full_title: PID Control for Feature Selection in Biomedical Datasets
venue: International Conference on Data Management, Analytics and Innovation (ICDMAI), Springer
card_text: Uses PID control to steer a population search for the best feature subset in biomedical data; on nine datasets it beat the Black Hole Algorithm, with 94.94% mean accuracy.
details_md:
## Abstract

Multi-dimensional biomedical datasets can contain hundreds or even thousands of features. Many of these are redundant, irrelevant, or noisy. Feature selection is an important step in reducing dataset complexity and increasing classification performance, and contributes to our knowledge in the domain. In this work, we propose Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control for feature selection in biomedical datasets. A population of candidate solutions is optimized via PID control to guide towards an optimal feature subset. We evaluate PID optimization combined with one of two mutation strategies: Flip-Bit and Levy-Flight Function mutation. The two PID variants are tested on nine biomedical datasets, and compared to the standard Black Hole Algorithm (BHA). PID control with flip-bit mutation achieves a mean accuracy of 94.94% for the datasets, with only 19.73% of total features used on average, outperforming BHA’s mean score of 94.53% with a higher feature usage percentage of 20.33% (less feature reduction). Lastly, PID control with Levy-Flight mutation scores a mean accuracy of 90.53%, but allows for the lowest feature usage (17.34%). Our results show that PID with flip-bit mutation achieves higher classification and better feature reduction than BHA, while PID with levy-flight mutation provides more feature reduction with a trade-off on accuracy.

card_title: ChatGPT didn't take me very far, did it?
full_title: ChatGPT Didn't Take Me Very Far, Did It?
venue: ACM Conference on Global Computing Education (CompEd), ACM, poster
card_text: A study of how students used ChatGPT in coursework, a semester-long project and summer internships; ChatGPT's answers fell into three classes, from immediately helpful to frustrating.
details_md:
## Abstract

The effect of ChatGPT (CG) on teachers, assessment and other matters have been discussed in many works, but no one appears to have studied how students are actually using it. We study how students use CG for coursework, a semester long project, and summer internships. We discover that from a student's perspective, CG responses fall into three classes: it is immediately helpful, it needs user help, or it leads to unhelpful frustration. We are developing a classification of these uses as a prelude to understanding how CG can contribute to improving student learning outcomes.

card_title: Symbolic reasoning and data-driven learning in human cognitive behaviour analysis: a review
full_title: Symbolic Reasoning and Data-Driven Learning in Human Cognitive Behaviour Analysis: A Review
venue: Chapter in Human Cognitive Behavioral Analysis using Deep Advanced Learning Techniques, CRC Press
card_text: A review chapter on how computers have been used to analyse human cognitive behaviour, tracing the shift from symbolic reasoning in the 1960s to data-driven learning from the 1990s.
details_md:
## Summary

This chapter reviews how computers have been used to analyse human cognitive behaviour, and how the field moved from symbolic reasoning to data-driven learning.

It traces the shift from the rule-based systems of the 1960s to the data-driven methods that took over from the 1990s, through early conversational models such as ELIZA and PARRY and diagnostic systems such as MYCIN, Psyxpert and BLUE-BOX. It sets out how the bottleneck moved from knowledge engineering in expert systems to feature engineering in classical machine learning.

It then looks at multimodal data fusion for affective computing, which combines physiological signals (EEG, ECG, GSR) with visual and audio data for emotion recognition and psychiatric monitoring.

The chapter is in press with CRC Press.

card_title: AI adoption and its influence on consumer behaviour: a review
full_title: AI Adoption and its Influence on Consumer Behaviour: A Review
venue: International Journal of Consumer Studies, Wiley
card_text: A review of how AI adoption shapes consumer behaviour, across recommendation systems, virtual assistants and predictive analytics, with trust and transparency as the main barriers to adoption.
details_md:
## Summary

This review asks how the adoption of AI is changing the way consumers behave, and what holds that adoption back. It brings together more than 40 studies of AI in consumer settings, including recommendation systems, virtual assistants and predictive analytics.

Across them, it finds trust, transparency and ethical concerns to be the main barriers to adoption, and it proposes a consumer-centric framework for deploying AI.

It also examines four real-world case studies of AI used to predict consumer behaviour, and how machine-learning models shape customer experience, personalised recommendations and brand loyalty.

The review is in press with the International Journal of Consumer Studies.

card_title: Using machine learning to predict depression in text
full_title: Using Machine Learning to Predict Depression in Text
venue: Symposium on Data Science for Smart Infrastructure, FLAME University, Pune, poster
card_text: A poster on detecting depression from Reddit posts: a curated dataset of Depression and Control posts, and a comparison of classifiers on TF-IDF features, reaching up to 91.06% accuracy.
details_md:
## Summary

I presented this poster at the Symposium on Data Science for Smart Infrastructure at FLAME University, Pune, in 2023. It set out early work on detecting depression from what people write online.

The poster presented a prototype dataset of Reddit posts, curated into Depression and Control classes, and compared several supervised classifiers trained on TF-IDF features, with accuracies of up to 91.06%. It closed with next steps: validating the dataset and moving to more advanced NLP methods.

The same line of work led to two papers: one with TF-IDF features and random forests at CSCT 2023, and one with word embeddings and sentence transformers in the Journal of Computational Social Science (2026).
